en: Of that howling infidel!
Break the withered spirit
Of that strutting infidel!
Stretch her out and thrash her like a hide!
Let her gather firewood and carry water;
Give that worn-out harlot
To the herdsman!”
The many wrestlers standing there
Cried, “Yes, sister-in-law, yes!”
And brought great misery upon the woman.
The wrestlers who received the command—
May God have cursed them long before—
Did to poor Akbala
Exactly as Chachykey
Had ordered:
They slit her crown and put worms in it,
Slit her soles and rubbed in salt,
Mounted her on a lanky mare,
And clothed her in a coarse felt coat.
The shepherd violated her by force,
The herdsman beat and violated her;
Not once, but a thousand times,
They committed horrors dreadful to know.
Upon Akbala’s head
They heaped not one torment but a thousand,
And brought her terrible misery;
Her noble head was enslaved.
Though a virtuous woman, she was beaten
And reviled by a scabby woman.
To think of it, those were dreadful days:
Kanykey and Akbala
Became slaves to Khan Kanchoro.
Day followed day,
Each passing in torment;
They sent Akbala barefoot
To follow behind the cows.
And poor Kanykey
They made tend the calves.
Let us leave this matter here
And begin again from another side:
Chürök, the moonlike woman—
Upon Chürök they heaped turmoil.
In the havoc inflicted upon Chürök,
Who showed regard for ancestral spirits?
Every one of the bloodthirsty hero’s countless treasures
They went and plundered, leaving nothing.
They seized all her silks,
And brought grievous misery;
They plundered all the gold
And inflicted bitter suffering.
Chürök became war-spoil—
Such was the havoc
The Jediger brought upon her.
In the mountains were ninety thousand horses,
But no swift courser or peerless steed;
After the mountain-like bloodthirsty hero,
No son remained!
On the hills grazed piebald horses,
With coursers and thoroughbreds among them;
There were fleet stallions, but no mares,
And to guard those horses
No heir of the bloodthirsty hero remained—
Such filth is this world!
Countless treasures and myriad possessions
Were seized by fools, who rose to power;
Alas, the precious world had gone awry,
And his poor mother was humiliated.
All the champions were beaten,
All the young wives were plundered,
While Kanchoro ruled the people,
Established in the palace.
Chürök, the moonlike woman,
The Jediger warrior Kyyaz
Had taken as war-spoil.
The myriad herds left by the bloodthirsty hero
He drove away in their entirety,
And every treasure of the lionhearted warrior
He plundered and carried off.
The Jediger raided,
Felling the plane trees,
Breaking down and toppling the palace;
Sixty women and widowed sisters-in-law
They noisily carried off as spoil.
They unleashed terrible misery,
And many households of orphans and widows
Beneath the wrath of warrior Kyyaz
Were slaughtered and left dead.
They cut down and felled the poplars,
Broke down and toppled the palace,
And utterly slaughtered
Every last guard.
If Chürök talked back,
They had devised a way to deal with her;
If she unexpectedly resisted,
If she chanced to answer back,
They would seize her and cut off her head,
Drag her along the road,
And hand her over to the Danggyt,
Gouge out both her eyes,
And if the wretch grew defiant,
Destroy and slaughter her—
Such was the Jediger’s intent.
Upon Chürök, the sunlike woman,
They brought anguish and calamity;
Upon Chürök, the moonlike woman,
They inflicted brutal oppression,
And plunged her into numbing misery.
On this side of Chürök
Stood black-hearted men,
Wrestlers crowding all around her.
When told to take a cap, they cut off a head—
Violent men surpassing ordinary mortals.
Looking to the other side,
There stood men in yellow rawhide trousers,
Each one able to face countless foes,
Their quivers bound and arrows counted,
Wrath blazing upon their faces
As though they would slaughter once again.
Looking upon this side,
They held spears without tassels,
Gripping the shafts greedily,
And thrusting them high aloft;
When battle was joined,
They never fearfully exposed their flanks.
When they moved, no living soul endured;
Whoever appeared before them
They crushed into earth as soft as felt.
Brandishing their spears,
Another band entered.
When she saw those wrestlers,
Your sister-in-law nearly died on the spot.
The valiant woman withered to a shadow,
As the many wrestlers bore down;
The crowd of wrestlers pressed mercilessly,
And when your sunlike, fierce sister-in-law
Suffered this guilty torment,
Her ribs felt torn apart,
Tears poured from her eyes,
And her heart was bitterly divided.
From shame she longed to die,
But the wretched woman could not,
For there was a child in her womb.
From shame she longed to depart,
But the wretched woman could not,
For she carried an unborn child.
She screamed and wept aloud;
Parted from her lionhearted hero,
She longed for death but could not die,
Unable to take her own life,
Unable to stem the tears from her eyes,
While her nose ran like a spring
And your sister-in-law could not wipe it away.
She wailed, “My bloodthirsty hero!”
“There is no cherished son to console me!
Oh, my mother!” she sobbed.
“The Creator has destined me for disaster,
And there is no choice but to bear it!
Among the many people, none can be my support;
The gray-maned hero left no son.
When grievous trouble befalls this forlorn head,
There is no choice but to endure it!
The birth mother of that gray-maned hero
Is, to me, the ill-fated Chürök,
The blessed brow of the noble one;
Above all, my mother
Is the Mecca of wretched Aichürök!”
If only I could see her, my heart would be at peace;
Apart from my mother, whom I took as my companion,
I have no one.
My insides burn, my liver is aflame;
I have burned and blazed to ashes.
My mature self has become spoil,
And I am going to the Jediger;
I have no mother to care for me!
Whom shall I hold as my Mecca?
The mainstay of the whole world—
Could my lion have come to this?
My blessed fortune, the White Matriarch—
Could my mother have come to this?”
Thus Aichürök,
Speaking sorrowfully, said these words.
Your sister-in-law whitened the dawn like an argali,
Speaking softly, saying this:
What recourse is there against humiliation?
Does not everyone have to submit
To the violence of the powerful?
Countless wrestlers surrounded her;
Against this Kyyaz, who fancied himself a god,
Even if a host encircled him, it could not prevail.
What could the helpless woman do?
Their khan issued his decree;
When the khan gave his command,
His wrestlers closed in.
Kyyaz’s violence
Surpassed all others in the world.
His demons had risen;
Good heavens, how hideous they looked!
Black-omened Kyyaz’s
Teeth were whetted,
And his power had grown immense.
He had diverted the waters of the Chüy;
Abandoning not merely his livestock
But even his own life,
The Jediger surged back again
And carried out savage plunder.
They slaughtered with fierce resolve;
Everything the eye could see
They gave over wholly to pillage.
The Jediger who descended upon you
Entered the white palace,
Dragging their whips behind them.
They spoke taunting words
And provoked the anger
Of Chürök, the formidable woman.
For the wretched prince’s wife
They dug a pit in the place of honor;
They scattered all four kinds of livestock.
The Jediger poured in without restraint
And broke open and searched the bundles;
Thus they stirred up needless strife.
They raided the mares from the hills
And cut off the head
Of the owner who came for his mare.
They forced out all the world’s bile,
Beating his brains from his skull.
They seized his camels as booty
And spilled the contents of his belly;
Thus did the Jediger act.
Crimson cloth in red patterns
They folded on the bias
And loaded upon red camels;
Crimson cloth mottled green
They folded beside the blood-red goods.
Pure gold and ruby stones
They loaded upon swift camels;
Loading each pack saddle with treasure,
They set out with all the wealth.
They dressed her in loose-flowing silk
And mounted her on an ambling pacer;
They dressed her in patterned silk—
Poor Chürök—
And mounted her on a sturdy pacer.
With horns and trumpets sounding,
Six thousand camels and forty pack saddles
Carried Aichürök’s countless possessions;
They loaded all her many treasures.
Red and green banners flew;
Such was the spectacle to behold.
A clamor split the sky,
And the wrestlers shouted;
The Jediger rejoiced,
Raising the battle cry “Kyyaz!”
Seeing the abundance of wealth,
The great riches left by the gray-maned hero,
The Jediger bustled about
And divided it by whip-lengths.
